public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Schur's theorem on Galois groups of truncated exponential polynomials

*Reference:* (https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2814220)

*Reference* (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/477077)
-/

@[expose] public section

/-
Note: This was asked by Nick Katz. Quasi-autoformalized using Claude 4.0 Sonnet.
-/

namespace SchurTruncatedExponential

open Polynomial

open scoped Nat

/--
The truncated exponential polynomial `truncatedExp n` is
given by `∑_{j=0}^{n} x^j / j!` over `ℚ`, which is the
`n`-th partial sum of the Taylor series for the exponential function `e^x`.
-/
noncomputable def truncatedExp (n : ℕ) : ℚ[X] :=
  ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), (1 / j ! : ℚ) • X ^ j

/--
**Schur's Theorem (1924):**
Let `f_n(x) = ∑_{j=0}^n x^j/j!` be the `n`-th truncated
exponential polynomial over `ℚ`. Then for `n ≥ 2`:

- If `n ≡ 0 (mod 4)`, the Galois group of `f_n` is isomorphic to the alternating group `A_n`
- If `n ≢ 0 (mod 4)`, the Galois group of `f_n` is isomorphic to the symmetric group `S_n`
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 12]
theorem schur_truncatedExp_galoisGroup_equiv (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≥ 2) :
  letI f := truncatedExp n
  if n % 4 = 0 then
    -- Galois group is alternating group A_n
    Nonempty (f.Gal ≃* alternatingGroup (Fin n))
  else
    -- Galois group is symmetric group S_n
    Nonempty (f.Gal ≃* Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) := by
  sorry

end SchurTruncatedExponential

findings.description: The theorem docstring opens with "**Schur's Theorem (1924):**", but Schur published this result in 1930 ("Gleichungen ohne Affekt"). His 1924 papers are unrelated: the three-part "Neue Anwendungen der Integralrechnung auf Probleme der Invariantentheorie". The irreducibility of f_n appeared in 1929. The Lean statement is unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: zbMATH JFM 56.0110.02 (https://zbmath.org/2562837, read via api.zbmath.org) records I. Schur, "Gleichungen ohne Affekt", Sitzungsberichte Akad. Berlin 1930, 443–449 (1930). The review says: "Der n-te Abschnitt der Exponentialreihe liefert in 1 + x/1! + x^2/2! + ⋯ + x^n/n! = 0 für jedes durch 4 teilbare n eine Gleichung, deren Galoissche Gruppe die alternierende Gruppe ist; für alle anderen n ist die Gleichung ohne Affekt." The zbMATH review of Coleman (Zbl 0672.12004, Enseign. Math. 33 (1987), 183–189) also cites "I. Schur, Sitzungsber. Akad. Wiss. Berlin 1930, 443--449 (1930; JFM 56.0110.02)". A zbMATH search for Schur's 1924 papers returns only the invariant-theory series.
findings.suggested_fix: Write "**Schur's Theorem (1930):**". Optionally cite the primary sources: I. Schur, Gleichungen ohne Affekt, Sitzungsber. Preuß. Akad. Wiss. Phys.-Math. Kl. (1930), 443–449; R. F. Coleman, On the Galois groups of the exponential Taylor polynomials, Enseign. Math. (2) 33 (1987), 183–189.

reformulations.difference: The sources' claim that "the Galois group of f_n is A_n / S_n" is about Gal(f_n) as a permutation group of the n roots. The Lean asserts only an abstract group isomorphism, `Nonempty (f.Gal ≃* alternatingGroup (Fin n))` or `Nonempty (f.Gal ≃* Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, and never mentions the action on the roots.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: f_n is separable of degree n. Its derivative is f_{n-1}, and f_n − f_{n−1} = x^n/n! with f_{n−1}(0) = 1, so f_n and f_n' are coprime. Hence Gal(f_n) acts faithfully on n distinct roots and embeds in S_n. An abstract isomorphism with S_n gives |Gal| = n!, so the embedding is onto. An abstract isomorphism with A_n makes the image a subgroup of index 2, and A_n is the only index-2 subgroup of S_n (Mathlib `Equiv.Perm.eq_alternatingGroup_of_index_eq_two`). The converse is immediate. I proved this in Lean with only standard axioms (scratch file /workspace/review/chain.lean, `Review.statement_iff_concrete`). For every n ≥ 2 the theorem body is ↔ `if n % 4 = 0 then (Gal.galActionHom (truncatedExp n) ℂ).range = alternatingGroup ((truncatedExp n).rootSet ℂ) else Function.Surjective (Gal.galActionHom (truncatedExp n) ℂ)`. The proof uses the proven lemmas `te_separable` and `te_natDegree`.

reformulations.difference: The sources state the theorem for every n with no lower bound (MO 477077: "S_n if n ≢ 0 mod 4 and A_n otherwise"; the Coleman/zbMATH review likewise). The Lean adds the hypothesis `hn : n ≥ 2`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The excluded cases are trivial. f_0 = 1 and f_1 = 1 + X split over ℚ, so their Galois groups are trivial, and so are A_0 = Perm(Fin 0) and S_1. I proved in Lean that the theorem body itself holds at n = 0 (the A_0 branch) and at n = 1 (the S_1 branch), in /workspace/review/small.lean. So `∀ n ≥ 2` is equivalent to `∀ n`.

review.notes:
The file has two declarations: `truncatedExp` and `schur_truncatedExp_galoisGroup_equiv`. Both match the cited sources and the primary literature (Schur 1930, JFM 56.0110.02; Coleman 1987, Zbl 0672.12004). The category `research solved` is correct, so there is no status issue. The only defect is the wrong year (1924) in the theorem docstring.

Lean checks (scratch files in /workspace/review/; all compiled with only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound):
- `truncatedExp` elaborates as `∑ j ∈ range (n+1), (1 / ↑(j !)) • X ^ j`. I checked `truncatedExp 1 = 1 + X` and `truncatedExp 2 = 1 + X + C (1/2) * X^2`.
- I proved that `truncatedExp n` has natDegree n, that its derivative is `truncatedExp (n-1)`, and that it is separable.
- I proved the abstract-isomorphism ↔ permutation-group equivalence (see reformulations).
- I proved the n = 2 instance end to end: `Review.n_two`, via `Gal.galActionHom_bijective_of_prime_degree`. It has exactly the type of `schur_truncatedExp_galoisGroup_equiv 2 le_rfl`, which confirms the statement is meaningful in its smallest case.
- The theorem body also holds at n = 0 and n = 1.

Other remarks:
- MO 477077's own open question is about truncated cosh polynomials (is the Galois group S_2 ≀ S_n?). It is not formalized here; the file uses that post only for its background statement of Schur's theorem, which it matches.
- The plain comment "This was asked by Nick Katz" is not supported by the cited pages (the math.SE question was asked by user 'Cubic Bear', the MO question by Orges Leka). It is not part of any statement.
